overview.title: Why one-hot vectors fail and what word embeddings are
overview.main_topic: The hidden assumption of one-hot encoding (all words are independent and orthogonal), the requirement that geometric distance reflect semantic distance, and the contrast between sparse hardcoded one-hot vectors and dense, learned, low-dimensional word embeddings (figure 14.3)
overview.central_idea: One-hot encoding is a feature-engineering choice that wrongly assumes every word is unrelated to every other. Word embeddings instead map words into a dense, low-dimensional, learned geometric space in which distances reflect meaning.
overview.importance: This page explains the failure of the one-hot LSTM on p.432 and gives the conceptual basis for the Embedding layer (14.5.3), pretrained embeddings (14.5.4) and the token embeddings of every Transformer later in the book.
learning_objectives: Explain why one-hot encoding is a feature-engineering decision with a built-in assumption
Show that distinct one-hot vectors are orthogonal and explain why that is wrong for words
State the goal of an embedding space: geometric distance should track semantic distance
Contrast one-hot vectors (binary, sparse, high-dimensional, hardcoded) with embeddings (dense, low-dimensional, learned)
Name typical embedding sizes (256, 512, 1,024) versus 30,000 for one-hot here
prerequisites: The one-hot LSTM and its poor result (pp.431-432)
The idea of a vocabulary and token indices (section 14.2)

summary:
The page draws the lesson from p.432: one-hot encoding words, the simplest option available, **wasn't a great idea**, and there is a better way, **word embeddings**.

**Section 14.5.2** explains why. One-hot encoding is a **feature-engineering decision**, and it injects an assumption about the feature space: that all tokens are **independent of each other**. Geometrically, one-hot vectors are all **orthogonal**. For words this is clearly wrong, because words form a structured space and share information. "Movie" and "film" are interchangeable in most sentences, so their vectors should be the same or nearly so, not orthogonal.

More abstractly, the **geometric relationship between word vectors should reflect the semantic relationship between the words**. Synonyms should get similar vectors, and in general the geometric distance (for example **cosine distance** or **L2 distance**) should relate to "semantic distance": unrelated words far apart, related words close together. **Word embeddings** are vector representations that do exactly this, mapping human language into a structured geometric space.

One-hot vectors are **binary, sparse and very high-dimensional** (as many dimensions as there are words in the vocabulary, 30,000 here). Embeddings are **low-dimensional floating-point (dense) vectors**, commonly 256-, 512- or 1,024-dimensional even for very large vocabularies. So embeddings pack more information into far fewer dimensions.

**Figure 14.3** shows this visually. On the left, four tall one-hot vectors, each almost entirely black (zeros) with a single white cell: *sparse, high-dimensional, hardcoded*. On the right, four short vectors with varied gray levels: *dense, lower-dimensional, learned from data*. The caption adds that hashing gives representations just as sparse and hardcoded as one-hot encoding.

paragraphs.what_it_says: One-hot encoding is a feature-engineering decision: it builds in the assumption that all tokens are independent, since one-hot vectors are mutually orthogonal. With one-hot vectors, the dot product of any two different words is 0 and every pair of different words is the same distance apart ($\sqrt{2}$). Whatever the model learns about "movie" therefore transfers nothing to "film"; it has to learn each word from scratch.

paragraphs.what_it_says: This printed paragraph begins in p433_e06 with "Whereas the vectors obtained through one-hot encoding". One-hot vectors are binary, sparse and as high-dimensional as the vocabulary, while embeddings are low-dimensional dense float vectors (figure 14.3). Embeddings of 256, 512 or 1,024 dimensions are common even for huge vocabularies, versus 30,000 dimensions for one-hot here. So embeddings pack more information into far fewer dimensions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In a dense vector every coordinate carries information, and the values are real numbers rather than 0/1. A 256-dimensional float vector can arrange tens of thousands of words with rich similarity structure, while a one-hot vector uses 30,000 slots to store a single integer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Dimensionality drives model size and speed. Replacing 30,000-dimensional inputs with, say, 64-256-dimensional ones is what cuts the model from 15M to 2M parameters on p.437.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: an embedding of dimension $k$ for vocabulary size $V$ is a $V\times k$ lookup table. Multiplying a one-hot vector by a $V\times k$ matrix gives exactly the same result, so an Embedding layer is mathematically a Dense layer with no bias on one-hot input, computed efficiently.

concepts.name: One-hot encoding of tokens
concepts.definition: A binary vector, as long as the vocabulary, with a single 1 at the token's index.
concepts.intuition: Each word gets its own private axis.
concepts.technical: Distinct one-hot vectors are orthogonal and equidistant, which encodes the assumption that all words are independent.
concepts.significance: This page identifies that assumption as the core flaw.
concepts.misconception: It is not assumption-free; it asserts that all words are equally unrelated.

concepts.name: Word embedding
concepts.definition: A dense, low-dimensional, learned floating-point vector representing a word, arranged so that geometric relations reflect semantic ones.
concepts.intuition: A map of meaning: similar words are neighbors.
concepts.technical: Typically 256-1,024 dimensions for large vocabularies; stored as a V×k table and learned from data.
concepts.significance: It fixes both the size problem and the independence assumption of one-hot vectors.
concepts.example: "movie" and "film" should map to nearly the same vector.
concepts.misconception: Embeddings are not hand-designed; their structure is learned from data (p.434).

concepts.name: Cosine and L2 distance
concepts.definition: Measures of how far apart two vectors are: the angle-based cosine distance and the Euclidean L2 distance.
concepts.intuition: Cosine asks whether two vectors point the same way; L2 asks how far apart their tips are.
concepts.technical: $\cos(u,v)=\frac{u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert}$; cosine distance $=1-\cos$; L2 $=\lVert u-v\rVert_2$.
concepts.significance: The book names both as candidate measures that should track semantic distance.
concepts.misconception: Cosine distance ignores vector length; two vectors can be far apart in L2 and still have cosine distance 0.

concepts.name: Feature engineering
concepts.definition: Choosing by hand how raw inputs are represented before learning.
concepts.intuition: Deciding which measuring tools the model gets to use.
concepts.technical: Every encoding implies structural assumptions about the input space.
concepts.significance: The authors reframe one-hot encoding as one such decision, and a poor one.
concepts.example: Choosing one-hot vectors asserts that all words are orthogonal.
concepts.misconception: Deep learning does not eliminate representation choices; it moves them (here, to learning the embedding).

math.title: One-hot vectors are mutually orthogonal
math.latex: e_i \cdot e_j = \begin{cases}1 & i=j\\ 0 & i\neq j\end{cases},\qquad \lVert e_i-e_j\rVert_2=\sqrt{2}\ (i\ne j)
math.source_text: one-hot vectors are all orthogonal to one another

variables.meaning: One-hot vector for token index i (length = vocabulary size)

math.operations: Dot product and Euclidean distance between standard basis vectors.
math.purpose: It makes precise the claim that one-hot encoding treats all words as independent.
math.interpretation: Every pair of distinct words is equally similar (0) and equally far apart ($\sqrt2$), whatever their meaning.
math.intuition: Each word sits at the end of its own axis, at right angles to all the others.
math.numerical_example: With V=4: e_movie=[0,1,0,0], e_film=[0,0,1,0]; dot product 0, distance √2 ≈ 1.414, the same as for movie vs. "banana".

math.title: Cosine distance and L2 distance
math.latex: d_{\cos}(u,v)=1-\frac{u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_2\,\lVert v\rVert_2},\qquad d_{L2}(u,v)=\lVert u-v\rVert_2=\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_k (u_k-v_k)^2}
math.source_text: the geometric distance (such as the cosine distance or L2 distance) between any two-word vectors
math.operations: Normalized dot product (cosine); root of summed squared differences (L2).
math.purpose: These are the geometric distances that, in a good embedding space, should correlate with semantic distance.
math.intuition: Synonyms should be neighbors on the map.

deeper.title: Embedding lookup equals one-hot times a matrix
deeper.body: Let $E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times k}$. For a one-hot $e_i$, $e_i^\top E = E_{i,:}$. So the first thing the p.432 LSTM did with its one-hot input, multiplying by its input kernels, was already an embedding lookup, just an enormously expensive one, spread across 4 gates × 2 directions and computed as a dense multiply over 30,000 zeros. An `Embedding` layer stores $E$ once and indexes into it directly. (Not in the book: this is why replacing one-hot encoding with an Embedding layer changes efficiency much more than expressiveness, which matches the unchanged ~84% accuracy reported on p.437.)

deeper.title: A map analogy
deeper.body: One-hot encoding is like giving every city its own dimension: Paris is 1 on the "Paris axis" and 0 everywhere else, so Paris is exactly as far from Lyon as from Tokyo. An embedding is like a real map with latitude and longitude: two coordinates, dense, and the distances mean something.

deeper.title: Counting the savings
deeper.body: A review of 600 tokens takes 600 × 30,000 = 18M numbers as one-hot (p.432), but only 600 × 256 ≈ 154k numbers as 256-dimensional embeddings, about 117 times fewer. (Illustrative arithmetic, not from the book.)

misconceptions.claim: One-hot encoding is a neutral, assumption-free way to feed words to a model.
misconceptions.correction: It assumes that all tokens are independent and equally dissimilar (orthogonal vectors), which is false for language.

misconceptions.claim: Higher-dimensional representations always carry more information.
misconceptions.correction: A 30,000-dimensional one-hot vector carries only one integer's worth of information. A 256-dimensional dense embedding packs in much more, namely relations between words.

misconceptions.claim: Embedding similarity must be measured with L2 distance.
misconceptions.correction: The book names cosine distance and L2 distance as examples; cosine is common because it ignores vector length.

takeaways: One-hot encoding is a feature-engineering choice that assumes all words are independent (orthogonal).
For language that assumption is wrong: "movie" and "film" should have nearly identical vectors.
In a good embedding space, geometric distance (cosine, L2) reflects semantic distance.
One-hot vectors are binary, sparse, vocabulary-sized and hardcoded; embeddings are dense, low-dimensional (256-1,024) and learned.
Embeddings pack more information into far fewer dimensions.

questions.question: What assumption does one-hot encoding inject about words, according to the page?
options: That all tokens are independent of one another
That frequent words are more important
That word order does not matter
That synonyms share the same index
questions.answer: That all tokens are independent of one another
questions.explanation: The text says one-hot encoding assumes tokens are independent, since their vectors are orthogonal. It says nothing about frequency, and word order is a separate matter (set vs. sequence models). Synonyms get different indices.

questions.question: Compute the dot product and the L2 distance between the one-hot vectors of "movie" (index 1) and "film" (index 2) in a 4-word vocabulary.
questions.explanation: [0,1,0,0]·[0,0,1,0] = 0, and the difference [0,1,-1,0] has norm √2. Any two distinct words give the same values, which is exactly the problem.

questions.question: List the three properties of one-hot vectors and the three of word embeddings shown in figure 14.3.
questions.answer: One-hot: sparse, high-dimensional, hardcoded. Embeddings: dense, lower-dimensional, learned from data.
questions.explanation: These are the labels and caption of figure 14.3.

questions.question: Why should a good embedding space make geometric distance relate to semantic distance? What does a model gain?
questions.answer: If similar words have similar vectors, whatever the model learns about one word automatically applies to its neighbors, so it generalizes from less data. With orthogonal vectors each word must be learned separately.
questions.explanation: This is the inference behind the authors' "movie"/"film" example. Linear layers respond similarly to similar inputs.

questions.question: Which embedding dimensionalities does the page call common for very large vocabularies?
questions.explanation: The text gives those numbers. 30,000 is the one-hot size for this vocabulary, 2D is only for toy plots (p.434), and vocabulary-sized vectors are one-hot.

questions.question: Name the two geometric distances the page offers as examples.
questions.explanation: They are mentioned in the second paragraph of 14.5.2.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend, in two sentences, why an Embedding layer should beat one-hot encoding for an LSTM?
questions.answer: Embeddings are small, dense and learned, so the model is faster and similar words can share what is learned. One-hot vectors are huge, sparse and treat every word as unrelated.
questions.explanation: Check yourself against the summary and figure 14.3.
